facts.claim: "Midnight Demon Club" is track 4 on Highly Suspect's fourth album The Midnight Demon Club, released 9 September 2022 on Roadrunner Records/FRKST.
The song was released as the title track and final pre-release single from the album, on about 6 September 2022, three days before the album came out.
The song's writing credits go to Drew Fulk, Johnny (John) Stevens, Rich Meyer and Ryan Meyer. Its production credits go to Drew Fulk and Highly Suspect.
The album was produced by Highly Suspect and WZRD BLD. Rich Costey mixed it, Mike Bozzi mastered it, and Mark Schwartz engineered it.
The album lineup is Johnny Stevens (vocals, guitar), Ryan Meyer (drums, vocals), Rich Meyer (bass, vocals), Matt Kofos (guitar) and Mark Schwartz (synths).

Johnny Stevens said the album is about becoming the best version of yourself after tragedy. He called it a second chance at life with a happier mindset, and said it is about having fun and keeping it moving because life is too short.
Stevens tied the album's themes to the death of a loved one, saying nothing sparks the imagination more than that.
The label describes the album as mixing metallic exorcism with hip-hop-influenced beat craft. AllMusic calls it a set that combined hip-hop beats and cinematic soundscapes with blazing metal.
A reviewer reported that the album's drums were recorded almost like a rap song because drummer Ryan Meyer was recovering from arm surgery.
The album failed to chart in the U.S., the band's first not to reach the Billboard 200 or the Rock and Hard Rock charts. Stevens later called it "trash" on X.

research.lineage: Highly Suspect work in modern alternative and hard rock, and on this album they blend heavy metal-leaning rock with hip-hop beat production, as the label and AllMusic describe it.

draft:
The fireflies show up first, keeping the narrator company for a smoke after dark, and that small, almost sweet image is the last gentle thing in **Midnight Demon Club** before the self-accounting starts. Then comes the chorus, which says the quiet part out loud: "I-I hate myself / But I'm loving this." Both halves are meant. The song doesn't ask you to pick one.

That's the feeling Highly Suspect build the track around: the odd pleasure of a bad night spent alone with your worst opinions of yourself. The sharpest line is "But I'm so good at judging it." It catches someone who can't fix their life but has become an expert critic of it, and who knows that's a dodge. The verses keep turning the knife on themselves. The narrator wishes someone could have been "more than just a friend," calls themselves a piece of shit, then adds that at least they understand it. Self-awareness becomes a kind of armor. When the narrator tells everyone else they're "so fucking great," it sounds less like praise than like a wall going up. Envy, longing and contempt sit in the same breath, and none of them wins. By the last chorus, "loving this" has slid into "feeling myself when my demons come out at night." The narrator never fixes anything. They just find the night more comfortable than the day.

The band plays it straight and loud. The drums drive a steady, fast beat with a hard snare and crashing cymbals, the bass digs a low line underneath, and the guitar grinds out a distorted riff that leans on sustained chords. The voice is raw and a little raspy, full-throated, and it breaks into shouts as the cymbals pile up. The production keeps the grit in, so the whole thing sounds thick and unscrubbed, which suits a song about not cleaning yourself up.

Drew Fulk co-wrote it with Johnny Stevens and the Meyer brothers, Rich and Ryan, and co-produced it with the band. It's the title track of the album Stevens described as a second chance at life after a death in his circle, a record about having fun because life is too short. In that light, "loving this" reads as a choice to enjoy the wreckage rather than drown in it. The writing can be blunt to a fault, and the demon chorus gets a little muddled in its middle lines. But the bluntness is also the point. Nobody talks to themselves in polished sentences at 2 a.m.

The song sticks because it lets you admit that tearing yourself apart can feel good, and it doesn't make you feel worse for liking it.
